 Trump’s Misguided Claim That ‘They’ Waited to Lower Gas Prices Until After the Midterms
 By Robert Farley 
 Posted on November 20, 2026 
 Gasoline prices have been trending downward, dropping about 75 cents per gallon since Sept. 24, though prices are still about 69 cents higher than this time a year ago.
 In a social media post on Nov. 17, President Donald Trump wrongly suggested there was a political motivation behind the falling prices to hurt Republicans in the midterms. “Biggest drop in gasoline in 18 years,” Trump wrote. “Notice that they waited until after the ‘Election?’”
 We reached out to the White House to find out whom the president meant by “they,” but we did not get a response. 
 For the drop in prices, the president’s post cited a Bloomberg columnist who posted on Nov. 12 that the previous two days were the largest one-day drops in retail gasoline prices in 18 years.
 Patrick De Haan , the head of petroleum analysis for the fuel-price tracking service GasBuddy, said that while those days did not represent the largest one-day drops in 18 years according to GasBuddy data, the decline was nonetheless “substantial.”
 However, the average retail price of gasoline had been steadily falling for more than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Indeed, the day before the election, Trump posted to social media, “Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK.” Oil prices are connected to gasoline prices because crude oil is the main component in gasoline. 
 In a press conference on Nov. 20, Trump said , “Crude oil prices have plummeted right since the end of the election. I wonder how that happened. Crude oil is down 20% since the start of November, and now it’s down to close to $80 a barrel. … It was a very big drop. Too bad we didn’t have that in front of the election, but that’s the way it goes.” In fact, as Trump’s post on Nov. 2 mentioned, the price of crude oil dropped from $110 a barrel on Oct. 19 to $100 the day before the election, according to the Energy Information Administration . It was at around $87 a barrel on Nov. 19.
 “The crude oil market began to ‘clean up’ early in the third quarter, and a lack of new US or Israeli initiatives in the Middle East has helped soften prices,” said Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil. “Even before that happened, crude prices normalized thanks to more crude from non-Middle Eastern sources, some modest global demand destruction, and the puzzling lack of Chinese buying that has been in the background for eight months.”
 Lower prices are also a seasonal phenomenon, he said.
 “The last 45-60 days of any year tend to bring inventory buildups for gasoline and diesel and we are now in the midst of that process,” Kloza said. “People drive less, refineries run hard, and it is typical for gas prices to bottom between Thanksgiving and the Epiphany” in early December.
 What’s new this year, he said, is “the wildcard of extraordinary profits for refiners making diesel and jet fuel.” Profits for those fuels are so large, he said, it is allowing refineries to make gasoline at a loss. 
 “So we are in a rendezvous with much cheaper prices,” Kloza said. “It has nothing to do with executive action but everything to do with history as well as the economics created by stunning profits for diesel and jet fuel. Simply put, gasoline in much of the country is a ‘loss leader’ for the entire refined barrel.”
 He expects prices to drop further, he said, because the markup for gasoline is currently much higher than normal.
 De Haan from GasBuddy agreed there is no “nefarious” political manipulation of prices.
 “There’s no they. It’s just the market,” De Haan said.
 “There’s no conspiracy,” he said.” It’s simply just that instead of solving the problem earlier, the president elected to not really address it permanently, and there’s a lot of back and forth on this. I mean, Trump before the election had suggested that he was not looking to escalate the situation with Iran.” And then after the election, he said that “he didn’t see a need for a deal with Iran. So he’s kind of virtue signaling both ways, and the market is just caught in this confusion of what’s going to happen.”
 Gasoline prices jumped between Labor Day, which was Sept. 7, and mid-September, De Haan said, largely due to refining issues in the U.S. interior. “Power outages at a Chicagoland refinery in early September started that huge surge, which then pulled in states in the Midwest in the Corn Belt” that also saw surges. “And then as those refining issues started to get sorted out, prices plateaued on Sept. 24th, and then they started to decline as those refining issues started to work their way out.”
 De Haan said the falling prices since late September are a combination of seasonal factors and the resolution of the refining issues. He also credits the U.S. military’s efforts in helping to shepherd oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
 “In addition, we also saw oil prices drop pretty precipitously in October as more oil was flowing through the Strait, and because in part the president hinted that he’s not looking for escalations between the U.S. and Iran,” De Haan said. “I mean that’s definitely part of it.”
 As for seasonal factors, De Haan said demand declines every fall.
 “Going back to the election in 2012, every election has seen gas prices drop in the 30-day run-up to it because it has nothing to do with the election, it has nothing to do with politics,” De Haan said. “It has everything to do with the fact that Americans drive less progressively as temperatures get cooler. We have made the switch back to winter gasoline. That happens in mid-September.”
 “Oil and gas prices are a function of a couple of dozen different levers,” De Haan said. “The president’s got a fairly small lever when it comes to pushing prices down, but arguably this time around, because his policy created a lever that pulled prices up [with the war in Iran], he would be able to pull that lever back down if he wanted to. But he didn’t really do that.”
 De Haan also expects prices to continue to come down in the short term.
 A customer uses a credit card to pay at the pump at a gas station in Los Angeles on Oct. 30. Photo by David Swanson / AFP via Getty Images. 
 “I think we’ll probably see the national average continuing to fall for another week, maybe two,” De Haan said. “We’re at $3.70 a gallon at this moment. … My guess is maybe $3.62 on Thanksgiving and maybe a little lower, but I think we’ll slide maybe to $3.45 to $3.55, and that’s where I see the decline then fading away. I think we probably won’t get much lower than $3.40 a gallon, unless there’s some sort of more definitive end to the U.S. and Iran [war] or Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. I think we’ll still remain elevated, but we’re narrowing that gap.”
 According to data from the Energy Information Administration, the national average for regular gasoline was about $3.63 per gallon for the week ending Nov. 16. That’s down from $4.34 the week ending Sept. 21. In Trump’s second term, the price fell to a low of $2.66 in mid-January before rising dramatically after the U.S. launched airstrikes against Iran in late February.
 Trump’s Use of Quotes for ‘Election’
 We also asked the White House what Trump meant by putting “Election” in quotes in his social media post. We got no response, but less than a week after the election, on Nov. 9, Trump posted , “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”
 But Trump has not provided any evidence to date of widespread voter fraud, nor the intentional manipulation of voting machines to produce different results.
 “There’s obviously no evidence of any kind of malfeasance or impropriety in the election,” David Becker , executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said in a press call the day after Trump posted his message.
 There were some “minor malfunctions” in some machines around the country, Becker said, which “happens sometimes to some degree in every election” and which were rectified. But, he said, “I have heard of no machine malfunctions that were significant or could have affected the outcome.” And because every state except Louisiana uses paper ballots, he said, it is possible to audit those ballots to ensure machines are functioning properly. 
 Becker noted that since Trump took office for his second term, the Department of Justice and FBI have analyzed and investigated voting machines and have produced no evidence of rigged election machines.

 Q: Are voting machines changing Democratic votes to Republican votes? Several posts on Facebook are making that claim. 
 A: There is no evidence that touchscreen voting machines are deliberately switching voter selections. Rather, elections experts and state election officials have said that reported issues of machines initially not recording votes correctly are a result of familiar machine calibration issues or voter error. Also, nearly the entire country votes in a manner where voters review a paper ballot before having their votes officially cast.
